html:
Mago was a Carthaginian who wrote a farming manual in Punic, said to fill 28 books. When Rome destroyed Carthage in 146 BCE, the Senate gave its libraries away but had Mago's work translated into Latin.

The book covered vines, olives, fruit trees, cattle and bees, and the running of large estates worked by slaves. It shows how productive the farms of the Carthaginian hinterland were. Roman writers on farming, such as Columella, called Mago the father of the subject and quoted him often.

The original is lost, and only quotations survive. It is one of the few works of Punic literature known at all. See also the farms of Roman Africa and Carthage and its fall.
